isaiah-53-rabbinic-messianic-reading: Isaiah 53 — really a passage that starts at 52:13 — describes a figure called 'my servant' who is despised, rejected, wounded, killed, buried with the rich, and afterwards sees light and is satisfied. Christians have pointed to it for two thousand years. The standard Jewish reply today is that the servant is the nation of Israel, not an individual. What most Christians do not know, and what makes this case worth reading first, is that this reply became standard relatively late — and that older Jewish sources read the same passage as being about the Messiah.
isaiah-53-servant-distinct-from-israel: If the servant of Isaiah 53 is the nation of Israel suffering at the hands of the nations, the Christian reading collapses. So this case does the close reading. Two details do most of the work: the servant is struck 'for the transgression of my people' — which is difficult if the servant *is* that people — and the servant is sinless, 'no violence, neither any deceit in his mouth,' which is not something the prophets ever say about Israel. Isaiah does elsewhere call Israel God's servant, so the question is a real one.
sukkah-52a-two-messiahs: The Hebrew Scriptures seem to describe the coming one twice, in ways that do not fit together: a conquering king from David's line who reigns in peace, and a servant who is despised, pierced and killed. This is not a Christian observation — the rabbis saw it too, and the Talmud resolves it by proposing two different Messiahs: Messiah son of Joseph, who is killed in battle, and Messiah son of David, who reigns. That solution exists inside Judaism because the problem is genuinely there in the text.
daniel-9-cut-off-before-destruction: Most prophecies can be placed almost anywhere in history, which is why arguing about them rarely settles anything. Daniel 9 is different because it has a sequence with a deadline in it: an anointed one is 'cut off,' and only *afterwards* do the people of a coming ruler destroy 'the city and the sanctuary.' The sanctuary — the Second Temple in Jerusalem — was destroyed by the Romans in AD 70. Whatever you make of the arithmetic of the seventy weeks, and that arithmetic is genuinely disputed, the order of events has an end point that has already passed.
micah-5-2-bethlehem: Micah, writing in the eighth century BC, says a ruler over Israel will come out of Bethlehem Ephratah — a village small enough to be worth naming as small — and adds that his 'goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting.' Two things are being claimed at once: a specific birthplace, and an origin that predates the birth. The counter-missionary reply focuses on the second half, arguing the Hebrew means ancient lineage rather than eternal existence, which is a fair question about the words.
zechariah-12-10-pierced: Zechariah 12 describes a day when God pours out a spirit of grace on Jerusalem, and says: 'they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him.' The verse is strange in Hebrew before anyone argues about it, because it shifts from 'me' to 'him' mid-sentence. What makes it worth a Christian's attention is not the Christian commentary on it but the Jewish commentary: the Talmud itself connects this mourning to a slain Messiah.
psalm-22-pierced-hands-feet: Psalm 22 opens with the words Jesus quotes from the cross and goes on to describe a man surrounded by enemies, his bones out of joint, his clothing divided by lot. Verse 16 is the disputed one. The standard Hebrew text reads something like 'like a lion, my hands and my feet'; the ancient Greek translation reads 'they pierced my hands and my feet.' This is a real textual question, not an obvious one, and pretending otherwise is how Christians lose credibility here — so the case lays out the manuscript evidence rather than asserting a reading.
genesis-49-10-shiloh: On his deathbed Jacob blesses his twelve sons and tells Judah that 'the sceptre shall not depart from Judah… until Shiloh come; and unto him shall the gathering of the people be.' Nobody is fully certain what the word 'Shiloh' means here — it is one of the genuinely obscure words in the Hebrew Bible. Ancient Jewish translations read it as a title of the Messiah. The argument turns on when Judah's governing authority actually ended, which is a historical question as much as a textual one.
isaiah-7-14-almah: This is the verse behind every Christmas reading: 'a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.' It is also the weakest of the famous Christian proof-texts, and this case says so up front. The Hebrew word is *almah*, which means a young woman of marriageable age; the specific word for virgin is *betulah*. The passage's immediate context is a sign to a king in the eighth century BC about a war that was about to end. Handle it as typology rather than as a knockdown prediction, or don't handle it at all.
second-temple-messianic-expectation: It is sometimes said that Christians invented the idea of the Messiah they wanted and then read it backwards into the Hebrew Bible. That claim can be checked, because we have Jewish writings from before Jesus was born — the Dead Sea Scrolls among them. They show a messianic expectation that was alive, specific and datable: a Dead Sea Scroll fragment describes a Messiah under whom the blind see and the dead are raised, which is almost exactly the answer Jesus later sends back to John the Baptist.
jeremiah-31-new-covenant: One of the most common objections is that Christianity invented a 'new covenant' to replace the one God made with Israel. The phrase, however, is not Christian in origin. It is Jeremiah's — a Hebrew prophet writing to Jewish people — and he says the new covenant will be made with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, by name: a covenant written on the heart, with sins remembered no more. That single verse dissolves the 'you made up a different religion' frame before it can form.
yoma-39b-forty-years: On the Day of Atonement the high priest drew lots between two goats, a crimson thread was said to turn white when the sacrifice was accepted, and a lamp in the Temple burned as a sign of God's presence. The Talmud — a Jewish source, not a Christian one — records that for the forty years before the Temple was destroyed in AD 70, the lot stopped coming up in the right hand, the thread stopped whitening, and the lamp went out. Forty years before AD 70 is AD 30.
atonement-after-the-temple: Leviticus 17:11 grounds atonement in blood placed on an altar: 'it is the blood that maketh an atonement for the soul.' The altar was in the Temple, and the Temple was destroyed in AD 70. Judaism has answered that gap for nineteen centuries with prayer, repentance and acts of kindness — a serious, ancient and deeply thought-through adaptation. This case asks the question underneath it, once and gently: what does the Torah itself say grounds atonement, and what happens when the thing it names is gone?
hosea-blindness-restoration-romans-11: Before any argument from any verse, a Christian has to deal with what Christians have done. Romans 11 is where the New Testament itself forbids it. Paul asks whether God has cast away his people and answers 'God forbid' — describing a partial and temporary blindness, an irrevocable calling, and a certain restoration, and warning Gentile believers explicitly not to boast against the root they were grafted into. This case exists because that chapter rules out the theology behind a millennium of violence.
nt-jewish-library: Many Jewish people encounter the New Testament as the founding document of the religion that persecuted their ancestors, which makes it very hard to read as anything else. This case sets that aside and looks at what the documents are: written almost entirely by Jews, arguing from the Hebrew Scriptures, about a Jewish teacher, largely for Jewish audiences, within a few decades of the events. That reading is not a Christian talking point — it is where a great deal of modern *Jewish* scholarship has landed.
avoid-talmud-quote-mining: You will find, very easily, lists of shocking quotations attributed to the Talmud, and they circulate widely in Christian and non-Christian settings alike. This case is about why using them will end your conversation and deserve to. The Talmud is a vast, argumentative, multi-voiced compilation in which minority opinions are recorded alongside the ones that were rejected — and most of the viral quotations are fabricated, mistranslated, or stripped of the context that reverses them. Their pedigree runs back to medieval forced-disputation propaganda.
avoid-jews-killed-jesus: The deicide charge — that the Jewish people as a people killed Jesus — is not merely tactless. It is the specific theological claim that supplied the vocabulary for the Rhineland massacres, the blood libel, the expulsions, and eventually for far worse. This case exists because the accusation is still in circulation in ordinary Christian speech, often without any awareness of what it is. It is also bad reading: a Roman prefect ordered the execution, and the New Testament's own account distributes the responsibility very differently.
avoid-legalism-caricature: Most Christians are taught, somewhere along the way, that Judaism is about earning God's favour through rule-keeping, and that Jesus and Paul came to replace that with grace. It is a caricature, it collapsed in scholarship half a century ago, and repeating it tells your Jewish friend that you have never actually asked them what they believe. Second-Temple Judaism was a religion of covenant grace with obligations attached — which is, incidentally, roughly what the New Testament describes as well.
avoid-gematria-bible-codes: Gematria assigns numerical values to Hebrew letters, and 'Bible codes' claim that skipping letters at fixed intervals reveals hidden messages. Both get used in Christian outreach as though they were evidence. This case is about why they are not: the same techniques applied to Moby-Dick or War and Peace produce equally striking 'predictions,' which is exactly what researchers demonstrated when the claim was tested. Using them signals that you cannot tell a pattern from a proof.
